response.root_problem: The duplicate rows are caused by missing database-enforced uniqueness and unsafe concurrent retry handling inside the transaction-owning monolith, not by the absence of a separate service.
constraints: Delivery is due in three days.
The monolith already owns the transaction boundary.
All callers rely on the existing response contract.
A new microservice would introduce distributed consistency, deployment, and contract-migration risk.
Existing data may already contain duplicate (payment_id, attempt) pairs.
response.tradeoffs: Keep retry handling in the monolith and make the smallest compatible correction: identify and reconcile existing duplicates, add a unique constraint or unique index on (payment_id, attempt), and make the transactional write idempotent by treating a uniqueness conflict as the existing retry result. This avoids a risky service extraction but postpones any broader architectural separation. It may add contention on the unique index, which is preferable to incorrect duplicate records and should be measured.
response.uncertainty: The stated facts do not reveal the database engine, current transaction isolation, duplicate-cleanup policy, or whether the response can be reconstructed deterministically after a uniqueness conflict. Those details affect implementation mechanics, but not the decision to avoid a three-day microservice extraction.
validation: Measure and classify existing duplicates before adding the constraint; define a reversible reconciliation procedure and retain an audit record.
Add concurrency tests that issue simultaneous retries for the same (payment_id, attempt) and verify exactly one row exists while every caller receives the established response shape and semantics.
Run existing contract and regression tests for all retry callers.
Test uniqueness-conflict handling, transaction rollback, timeouts, and repeated requests under production-like concurrency.
Deploy incrementally with duplicate-rate, conflict-rate, latency, error-rate, and database-lock monitoring.

Rollback application logic to the prior version if error or latency thresholds regress; retain the uniqueness constraint when compatible because it protects data integrity, but prepare a reviewed reversible migration if it must be removed. Do not restore reconciled duplicates; preserve their audit/backup data.
